item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q020_syntaxin_fragment_reclassification","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 should not be read as saying that the short 1br0 and 1ez3 constructs independently define a separate biological fold. In the current release, 1br0 chain A (d1br0a_), all three 1ez3 syntaxin chains (d1ez3a_/b_/c_), and the full syntaxin chain 1dn1B (d1dn1b_) are all classified as a.47.2.1: class a, All alpha proteins; fold a.47, STAT-like; superfamily a.47.2, t-snare proteins; family a.47.2.1, t-snare proteins. The sequence records make the fragment issue explicit: 1br0 is 120 residues, 1ez3 chains are 124 residues, while 1dn1B is 222 residues. Thus the fragment assignments are best interpreted as partial structural observations anchored by the full syntaxin N-terminal domain assignment, not as independent evidence that a fragment alone transfers the whole-domain fold, boundaries, or function. Homology/function transfer is strongest at the t-SNARE family/superfamily level for the syntaxin domains, but fold-level similarity to STAT-like proteins should not be overread as close evolutionary or functional equivalence. For template or representative choice, a full-domain syntaxin representative such as 1dn1B is biologically safer than 1br0/1ez3 fragments; the fragments may support local all-alpha helical packing only. Also, 1dn1 chain A must be kept separate: SCOPe classifies it as e.25.1.1, Sec1/Munc18-like proteins, in the multi-domain alpha-and-beta class, so no syntaxin a.47.2.1 fold/function assignment should be transferred to that binding partner. Older SCOP 1.55 already placed 1br0, 1ez3, and 1dn1B at a.47.2.1, so the practical change in interpretation is not a new fold label but a corrected biological caution: fragment-based assignments should be treated as provisional/partial unless supported by the full domain and by release-specific SCOPe hierarchy
